definition:
Faith, in the Bible's sense, is trust in God and in what he has promised. It is not a leap in the dark, and it is not a feeling that grows stronger the less evidence it has. It is the answer a person gives to someone who has spoken and has proved reliable. Abraham is the pattern: God promised him descendants as many as the stars, and “Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6). Faith looks away from itself to the God who promises, which is why Hebrews can call it “the assurance of what we hope for and the certainty of what we do not see” (Hebrews 11:1): it rests on God's word about things not yet in view. In both testaments that trust does not stay private. It shows itself in obedience, in endurance under trial, and in hope that waits for what God has not yet done, so that the Bible's one word covers both believing and being faithful. Faith is how a person receives salvation; the verdict it receives (justification) and the turning that always accompanies it (repentance) have their own studies.

The Hebrew vocabulary centers on the root 'aman, ‘to be firm, reliable, lasting’. In its causative stem the verb he'emin means to hold something firm, that is, to believe or to trust, and its first appearance in the Bible is Genesis 15:6. The same root gives 'emunah, ‘steadiness, faithfulness’, used once of Moses' hands held steady (Exodus 17:12) and far more often of God's own reliability, and it gives the word amen, ‘surely, so be it’. Alongside it stand batach, ‘to trust, to feel secure’ (about 120 times, nearly half of them in the Psalms), and chasah, ‘to take refuge’. The New Testament uses the noun pistis and the verb pisteuō, each about 240 times, and the adjective pistos, ‘faithful, trustworthy’. In ordinary Greek pistis meant trust, the trustworthiness that invites trust, and even a pledge or proof; it is the word behind ‘proof’ in Acts 17:31 and ‘faithfulness’ in Matthew 23:23. Context decides which sense a verse carries, and no English word covers them all, which is why ‘faith’, ‘belief’, ‘trust’, and ‘faithfulness’ all translate one Greek family.
ot:
Faith enters the Bible's story with a man leaving home on the strength of a promise. God called Abram out of Haran with nothing but a word about land, descendants, and blessing for all nations (Genesis 12:1-3), and Abram went. Years later, still childless, he complained that the promise had come to nothing, and God took him outside to count the stars. The narrator's comment, “Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6), is the first use of he'emin in Scripture, and it comes before any covenant ritual, before circumcision, and centuries before the law. The same Abraham doubts, schemes with Hagar (Genesis 16), and laughs at the promise alongside Sarah (Genesis 17:17; 18:12). Biblical faith is not a flawless mood. It is a settled reliance on God that is tested and deepened, and at Moriah, where Abraham tells his son “God Himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering” (Genesis 22:8), the test is as severe as any in the Bible.

The exodus teaches what faith is by showing its opposite. When Moses and Aaron first bring God's word to the enslaved Hebrews, “they believed” (Exodus 4:31), and after the sea “the people feared the LORD and believed in Him and in His servant Moses” (Exodus 14:31). Within weeks the same people grumble for water and bread. At the edge of Canaan, after the spies' report, God asks, “How long will they refuse to believe in Me, despite all the signs I have performed among them?” (Numbers 14:11), and Moses later says the generation that died in the wilderness “did not trust the LORD your God” (Deuteronomy 1:32). Even Moses is barred from the land because “you did not trust Me” (Numbers 20:12). Unbelief in the Old Testament is rarely a matter of intellectual doubt about God's existence. It is a refusal to rely on a God who has already shown himself reliable, a failure of memory as much as of nerve; Psalm 106:12-13 captures it in two lines, “Then they believed His promises and sang His praise. Yet they soon forgot His works.”

In the kingdom period faith becomes a political question. When Syria and the northern kingdom threatened Jerusalem, around 735 to 734 BC, Isaiah met King Ahaz and told him, “If you do not stand firm in your faith, then you will not stand at all” (Isaiah 7:9). The Hebrew is a play on the root 'aman ('im lo ta'aminu ki lo te'amenu), roughly ‘if you will not hold firm, you will not be held firm’. Ahaz chose instead to buy the protection of Assyria (2 Kings 16:7-9). Isaiah later spoke of a stone God would lay in Zion, “a sure foundation; the one who believes will never be shaken” (Isaiah 28:16), a text Paul and Peter both apply to Christ (Romans 9:33; 1 Peter 2:6). Jehoshaphat's charge to his army uses the same root (2 Chronicles 20:20), and of Hezekiah the historian says simply, “Hezekiah trusted in the LORD” (2 Kings 18:5). The Psalms turn this into prayer: “When I am afraid, I put my trust in You” (Psalm 56:3). Proverbs sets trust against self-reliance (Proverbs 3:5), and in Daniel three exiles show faith that obeys without a guarantee of rescue, “even if He does not” (Daniel 3:18).

Habakkuk, writing as Babylon rose in the late seventh century BC, asked how God could use a cruel empire to judge Judah. The answer he received was to wait for a vision that would surely come, and it contains the line “the righteous will live by faith” (Habakkuk 2:4). The Hebrew word is 'emunah, steadfast faithfulness: the righteous person survives the coming disaster by holding firm to God. The Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures made by Jews from the third century BC) reads ‘by my faithfulness’, pointing to God's reliability, while Paul quotes the line without a pronoun, and interpreters still discuss how the Hebrew and Greek forms relate. Habakkuk's book ends with a farmer's confession that he will rejoice in God even when the fig tree does not bud (Habakkuk 3:17-18). Beneath all human faith in the Old Testament lies God's own faithfulness. Moses calls him “a God of faithfulness without injustice” (Deuteronomy 32:4), and after Jerusalem fell in 587 or 586 BC, a poet sitting in its ruins could still write, “great is Your faithfulness” (Lamentations 3:23). Faith is the fitting answer to a faithful God, and it is not confined to Israel: when Jonah preached, “the Ninevites believed God” (Jonah 3:5).
nt:
Jesus opened his ministry with a double command, “Repent and believe in the gospel” (Mark 1:15), and faith runs through his work. He tells a healed woman, “your faith has healed you” (Mark 5:34), and a forgiven one, “Your faith has saved you; go in peace” (Luke 7:50). He marvels at the faith of a Roman centurion (Matthew 8:10) and of a Canaanite mother (Matthew 15:28), both outsiders, and rebukes his own disciples as people “of little faith” (Matthew 6:30; 14:31). In the Gospels faith is not a force the believer generates. It is reliance on Jesus himself, which is why even a mustard seed of it is enough (Matthew 17:20), and why a desperate father can pray, “I do believe; help my unbelief” (Mark 9:24), and be answered. Jesus also asks whether the Son of Man will find faith on earth when he comes (Luke 18:8), tying faith to endurance until the end.

John's Gospel never uses the noun pistis, but it uses the verb pisteuō nearly a hundred times, often with the preposition eis, ‘believing into’ Jesus, a construction that stresses personal attachment rather than bare agreement. John states his purpose plainly: the signs “are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in His name” (John 20:31). Faith in John has content (Martha's confession, “I believe that You are the Christ, the Son of God,” John 11:27), and it has an object who can be trusted with life and death (John 11:25-26). Believing is receiving Christ (John 1:12), it is the one “work” God asks for (John 6:29), and it reaches its climax in Thomas's confession, “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28), with a blessing on all who believe without seeing (John 20:29). In Acts the apostles' message is summarized, “Believe in the Lord Jesus and you will be saved” (Acts 16:31), and the new movement can be called simply “the faith” (Acts 6:7; 14:22).

Paul made faith the hinge of his gospel. Righteousness from God is revealed “by faith from start to finish” (Romans 1:17), and it comes to “the one who does not work, but believes in Him who justifies the wicked” (Romans 4:5). Abraham is his proof: he was “fully persuaded that God was able to do what He had promised” (Romans 4:21), even when his own body said otherwise. Faith for Paul is the opposite of boasting, not of effort; it receives what God gives, and “faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of Christ” (Romans 10:17). Yet Paul's aim is “the obedience that comes from faith” (Romans 1:5), and he can say that what counts is “faith, expressed through love” (Galatians 5:6). Faithfulness appears in his list of the Spirit's fruit (Galatians 5:22). A long-running scholarly question concerns the Greek phrase pistis Christou (Galatians 2:16; Romans 3:22; Philippians 3:9), which can be read as ‘faith in Christ’, as most modern translations do, or as ‘the faith (or faithfulness) of Christ’, as the King James Version rendered it. Richard B. Hays argued for the second reading in The Faith of Jesus Christ (1983), while James D. G. Dunn and others defended the first; both readings affirm that believers are saved by trusting Christ, and they differ on what these particular verses emphasize. Whether faith itself is God's gift is also debated: Ephesians 2:8 says “it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God,” and interpreters differ over whether ‘this’ refers to faith or to the whole of salvation, while Philippians 1:29 speaks of believing as something ‘granted’.

Hebrews and James press the same faith into the long run. Hebrews 11 defines faith by its grip on unseen realities and then shows it at work in a gallery of Israel's history, from Abel to the prophets. Its heroes obeyed, went out, endured, and many “died in faith, without having received the things they were promised” (Hebrews 11:13). The chapter ends by pointing to Jesus, “the author and perfecter of our faith” (Hebrews 12:2), who endured the cross. James warns that a faith consisting only of correct belief is no better than the demons' belief, who “believe that—and shudder” (James 2:19), and concludes that “faith by itself, if it does not result in action, is dead” (James 2:17). Peter describes faith refined by trial like gold (1 Peter 1:7), John calls faith the victory that overcomes the world (1 John 5:4), and Jude speaks of “the faith entrusted once for all to the saints” (Jude 3), the content believed. Revelation closes the canon with a call to be “faithful even unto death” (Revelation 2:10) and names the returning Christ “Faithful and True” (Revelation 19:11). The faithfulness that began with God's promise to Abraham ends in the faithful one himself.

keyTexts.why: The first use of the Hebrew verb for believing. Abram trusts God's promise and it is counted to him as righteousness, before circumcision and before the law. Paul, James, and Hebrews all return to this verse.
After the sea, Israel fears the LORD and believes in him. Faith is response to God's saving act, and the wilderness chapters that follow show how quickly it can fail.
God names Israel's refusal to enter the land as unbelief despite all his signs. Unbelief in Scripture is a refusal to rely on a God who has proved reliable, not only an intellectual doubt.
Isaiah's wordplay on the root 'aman tells Ahaz that only those who hold firm to God will be held firm. Faith is set against political self-reliance.
The righteous will live by faithfulness while waiting for God to act. Paul quotes it in Romans 1:17 and Galatians 3:11, and Hebrews 10:38 uses it to call for endurance.
A father's cry, “I do believe; help my unbelief,” is answered by Jesus. Faith in the Gospels can be weak and mixed with doubt and still reach out to Christ.
Thomas moves from doubt to confessing Jesus as Lord and God, and John states that his Gospel was written so that readers may believe and have life.
Abraham is fully persuaded that God can do what he promised, against the evidence of his own body. Faith rests on God's power and promise, and so salvation rests on grace.
Faith believes in the heart that God raised Jesus and confesses him as Lord, and it comes by hearing the word of Christ. Faith has content and is created through the message.
What matters in Christ is faith expressed through love. Paul, who insists that justification is by faith and not by works of the law, insists just as firmly that true faith works.
Salvation is by grace through faith, not from ourselves, not by works, so no one may boast, and believers are created for good works. The interpretation of ‘this’ in verse 8 is debated.
The Bible's fullest portrait of faith: confidence in God's promise, shown in obedience and endurance by people who died before receiving what was promised, and completed in Jesus.
A faith that produces no deeds is dead, and even demons believe that God is one. James guards against treating faith as bare assent.
Faith is tested like gold in fire, loves a Christ it has not seen, and receives salvation as its goal. Faith and hope are bound together.
The risen Christ calls a suffering church to be faithful even unto death. At the end of the canon faith is fidelity under pressure.

history:
The early church spoke of faith as the entrance to the Christian life and as the content confessed in baptism. The creeds themselves begin with the words ‘I believe’ or ‘we believe’: the Apostles' Creed grew from the Roman baptismal confession, and the Nicene Creed (325, expanded at Constantinople in 381) sets out what the church believes. Clement of Rome, writing around AD 96 (1 Clement 32 and 33), taught that believers are justified through faith and not by their own works, and in the same breath urged them to good works. Augustine of Hippo distinguished believing that God exists, believing what God says, and believing into God, the last meaning to cleave to him in love (Tractates on John 29.6), a distinction that medieval theologians took up. Against the followers of Pelagius, who held that human beings can obey God by their natural powers, the Council of Orange (529) taught that even the beginning of faith is a gift of grace and not a product of human nature.

Medieval theology treated faith as the first of the three theological virtues named in 1 Corinthians 13:13. Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae II-II, questions 1 to 16, written around 1270) defined faith as an act of the intellect assenting to divine truth, moved by the will under grace, and taught that faith is made living, or ‘formed’, by love, so that faith without charity is real but lifeless. The Reformers challenged this framework. Martin Luther taught that faith is a living, bold trust in God's grace that unites the believer to Christ and justifies apart from works, though it cannot fail to produce them; Philip Melanchthon's Apology of the Augsburg Confession (1531, Article IV) insisted that justifying faith is not mere knowledge of history but trust in the promise of mercy. John Calvin (Institutes 3.2, 1559) defined faith as a firm and certain knowledge of God's benevolence toward us, founded on the promise in Christ, revealed to the mind and sealed on the heart by the Spirit. The Heidelberg Catechism (1563, Question 21) calls true faith both a sure knowledge and a wholehearted trust, and the Westminster Confession of Faith (1646, chapter 14, ‘Of Saving Faith’) describes it as the work of the Spirit, ordinarily produced by the ministry of the word, whose principal acts are accepting, receiving, and resting on Christ alone. Later Protestant theologians, Lutheran and Reformed, analyzed faith as knowledge (notitia), assent (assensus), and trust (fiducia).

The Council of Trent answered in its Decree on Justification (1547), teaching that faith is the beginning of human salvation and the foundation and root of all justification, and rejecting the claim that justifying faith is nothing but confidence in God's mercy. The First Vatican Council, in Dei Filius (24 April 1870), defined faith as a supernatural virtue by which, with God's grace, we believe what he has revealed to be true because of the authority of God who reveals it, and it rejected both the rationalism that makes faith unnecessary and the view that faith is blind. The Eastern Orthodox Confession of Dositheus, adopted by a synod at Jerusalem in 1672, stated that a person is justified not by faith alone but by faith working through love. John Wesley, after hearing Luther's preface to Romans read in London on 24 May 1738, preached salvation by faith as trust and taught that the Spirit gives believers an inward witness to their adoption.

Later debates have tested the boundaries. The Scottish writer Robert Sandeman taught in the eighteenth century that saving faith is bare belief of the bare truth, and the English Baptist Andrew Fuller answered him in Strictures on Sandemanianism (1810), arguing that saving faith includes the heart's affection for God. In the late 1980s American evangelicals, many of them Baptists and dispensationalists, argued over ‘lordship salvation’: John MacArthur's The Gospel According to Jesus (1988) was answered by Zane Hodges's Absolutely Free (1989) and Charles Ryrie's So Great Salvation (1989). Biblical scholarship has meanwhile renewed attention to faith as relational trust and loyalty, including Teresa Morgan's Roman Faith and Christian Faith (2015) and Matthew W. Bates's Salvation by Allegiance Alone (2017), which proposes ‘allegiance’ as a better English equivalent for pistis in many contexts, a proposal that has drawn both support and criticism.

differ.view: Trust that receives Christ (Lutheran and Reformed)
differ.body: Lutheran and Reformed churches teach that saving faith is knowledge of the gospel, assent to it, and above all trust in Christ and the promise of mercy. Faith justifies not because it is a virtue God rewards but because it receives Christ and his righteousness, like an empty hand. It is God's gift, created by the Spirit through the word (Romans 10:17) and, in Lutheran teaching, also through the sacraments. Faith alone justifies, but the faith that justifies is never alone: it lives, loves, and works, because it unites the believer to Christ. Defenders point to Romans 4:5, where God justifies the one who does not work but believes, and to Ephesians 2:8-9, and they hold that making love part of what justifies would turn the believer back to his own progress for assurance. Reformed theology adds that faith follows regeneration and flows from God's electing grace; Lutherans generally decline to build a logical order of that kind and stress the power of the word and sacraments to create faith. Many Baptists hold this account in its Reformed form.

differ.view: Faith enabled by prevenient grace (Wesleyan and Arminian)
differ.body: Wesleyan and Arminian Christians agree that fallen people cannot believe by their own power and that faith is not a meritorious work. God's prevenient grace, the grace that goes before, is extended to all, awakening conscience and restoring the ability to respond to the gospel or to resist it. Saving faith is then a real human trust, enabled by grace and freely given, by which God justifies and regenerates the sinner, and the Spirit ordinarily grants an inner assurance of adoption (Romans 8:16). Because grace can be resisted, faith is a living relationship that must be kept, and Scripture's warnings against unbelief are real (Hebrews 3:12). Defenders point to the universal calls to believe (Acts 17:30; John 3:16), to texts where people resist the Spirit, and to the sincerity of God's offer. Many General Baptists and Free Will Baptists, as well as Methodists, Nazarenes, and most Pentecostals, hold this view.

Catholic teaching holds that faith is a supernatural gift and virtue by which a person, moved by grace, assents to everything God has revealed because of God's authority, and entrusts himself to God. Faith is the beginning, foundation, and root of justification, but a person is justified when faith is joined with hope and charity, since what counts is “faith, expressed through love” (Galatians 5:6), and the greatest of the three is love (1 Corinthians 13:13). Faith without charity is real but dead (James 2:17). Faith is ordinarily received in baptism, grows through the sacraments and obedience, and is believed within the church, which hands on the content of the faith. Defenders point to James 2:24, to Paul's ‘obedience of faith’, to Augustine and Aquinas, and to the Council of Trent. The Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (1999) holds that Catholics and Lutherans share a basic consensus that salvation is by grace through faith, while differences remain.

differ.view: Faith as living trust and faithfulness (Eastern Orthodox)
differ.body: The Orthodox churches treat faith as trust in and faithfulness to the Triune God, lived within the church's worship, sacraments, and ascetic life. They resist separating believing from doing, or declaring righteous from making righteous, and read the New Testament through the Greek fathers, for whom salvation is union with God and participation in his life by grace (2 Peter 1:4). Faith is a synergy, God's grace and human freedom working together, never an independent human achievement and never a passive receiving that excludes cooperation. The Confession of Dositheus (1672) states that a person is justified by faith working through love. Defenders argue that this keeps faith, love, and obedience together as the New Testament does, and that the Western arguments over faith alone rest on assumptions the East never shared.

differ.view: The lordship and free grace debate (evangelical)
differ.body: Within evangelical churches, especially Baptist and dispensational ones, two views differ on what saving faith includes. Lordship theologians, such as John MacArthur, hold that saving faith receives Jesus as both Savior and Lord, so that it includes repentance and a submission of the will, and that a professed faith with no change of life was never saving faith (James 2:17; Luke 14:25-33). They hold that the faith is still God's gift and not a work. Free grace theologians, such as Zane Hodges and Charles Ryrie (who differed from each other on details, including repentance), hold that saving faith is trusting Christ's promise of eternal life, so that adding submission or a changed life as a condition confuses justification with discipleship and makes assurance impossible. They affirm that God calls every believer to obedience and disciplines the disobedient, but hold that eternal life is given at the moment of faith (John 5:24; 6:47). Each side sees itself as guarding the gospel of grace.

errors:
The church has rejected accounts of faith that make it smaller than Scripture does. One makes faith a human achievement, the contribution sinners bring to God in exchange for grace; the Council of Orange (529) rejected this in its Pelagian and semi-Pelagian forms, teaching that even the beginning of faith is God's gift, and Protestant and Catholic teaching alike deny that faith merits salvation. Another reduces faith to bare assent, believing correct statements while trusting and loving nothing; James answers that the demons believe as much (James 2:19), and Andrew Fuller answered the Sandemanians on the same ground. The opposite error cuts faith loose from content, as though sincerity alone mattered and it did not much matter what, or whom, one trusted. The New Testament's faith has an object, Jesus Christ crucified and raised, and a content that can be confessed (Romans 10:9; Jude 3).

A fourth distortion treats faith as a force that obtains what it wants: the more intensely one believes, the more health and wealth God is bound to give, and illness or poverty is a sign of weak faith. The Gospels' mustard seed teaches the opposite, that faith's power lies in its object and not its size, and Hebrews 11 praises believers who were tortured, impoverished, and killed without receiving what was promised. Finally, faith is not the opposite of reason or evidence. Scripture grounds it in God's acts in history, the exodus, the return from exile, and the resurrection of Jesus, which Paul says God has given as proof to all (Acts 17:31), and the church has generally held, against both rationalism and fideism, that faith goes beyond what reason can prove without contradicting it.
life:
Faith changes where a person looks. Anxiety keeps its eyes on the problem, and scrupulous religion keeps its eyes on the quality of its own believing. Biblical faith looks at God and at what he has said. That is freeing for people who fear their faith is too weak: the father in Mark 9 had a mixed and struggling faith, and Jesus answered it. Faith grows the way trust between persons grows, by hearing and remembering what the other has said and done, which is why Scripture keeps retelling the exodus and why the New Testament ties faith to hearing the word (Romans 10:17). Prayer is faith speaking, and the Psalms show that it can speak with complaint and fear as well as praise.

Because the Bible's word for faith is also its word for faithfulness, faith shows up in ordinary fidelity: keeping promises, staying at a hard post, telling the truth when it costs. Hebrews 11 is a list of people who acted on what God had said, often without seeing the outcome. Faith also gives a way to endure what does not resolve. Habakkuk's farmer rejoices with an empty fold, the three in Babylon say “even if He does not,” and many in Hebrews 11 die still waiting. Faith does not deny the darkness. It holds to the God who has promised morning, and it hopes for what God has not yet done.
questions: Genesis 15:6 comes between Abraham's complaint and his later scheme with Hagar. What does his story show about the relation between faith and doubt?
Paul says we are justified by faith apart from works, and James says faith without works is dead. How do the two fit together, and why might each have needed to say what he said?
Where in your own life does trust in God need to show itself as faithfulness, in a promise kept, a place stayed, or a hope held when nothing has changed?
